catalog_quote: 2.2.4. Tons. La langue des Basoa atteste des tons simples et des tons complexes. Tons simples. Phonologiquement, il n’existe donc que le ton haut et le ton bas. Sur le plan phonétique pourtant on peut percevoir trois tons simples: haut, moyen et bas. Le ton haut est symbolisé par l’accent aigu (´), le ton bas par l’absence de tout signe et le ton moyen par le singe (˘). Ce dernier doit être décrit comme un ton descendant bref ... Le ton moyen, comme on peut le constater à l’aide des exemples (33); n’est en effet, que la réalisation du ton haut dans la suite °HB. ... Tons complexes. Il s’agit du ton montant (ˇ) et du ton descendant (ˆ). En principe, ces tons complexes sont les produits d’application des règles de contraction ... Les exemples (34c) indiquent la valeur lexicale des tons en soa. c. moto ‘homme’ vs. motó ‘tête’ ... mwélá ‘fumée’ vs. mwĕla ‘queue’. (p. 24) — 6.4. Orientations pour la recherche future. ... Elle pourrait peut-être renseigner sur l’origine des phénomènes prosodiques assez caractéristiques qu’on observe dans cette région de la courbe du Fleuve et dont l’aire s’étend jusqu’aux Batetela. Il s’agit, par exemple, en dehors de la tonologie d’un système de stresses (ou rythmique ?) consistant à « traîner » dans la réalisation de certaines unités prosodiques. Ce système n’a malheusement encore fait l’objet d’aucune étude. (p. 243)

new_statements.quote: 4.1. Gesogo is a language with lexical tone. The alternance of tone on verbal radicals is hidden in the infinitive, but is regularly observed in both affirmative and negative tenses. 4.2. Nominals can be classified into four tone-groups according to the tone of the radical and suffix. 4.3. The tone-pattern of words is maintained in all observed syntactical positions. 4.4. An acute accent (´) marks a high tone, and an unmarked syllable denotes a normal low tone. A circumflex accent (^) indicates a falling tone, and an inverted circumflex accent denotes a rising tone. A mid-tone is a slipped high tone and is marked with a grave accent (`).

new_statements.rule_in_words: The language has lexical tone (high, low, falling, rising, and a 'slipped high' mid tone); nouns fall into four tone classes by radical+suffix tone and word tone patterns are stable across syntactic positions. No word stress is described anywhere in the sketch; the only 'accents' are tone diacritics. Stoop 1989 (pp. 130, 132) independently treats the language as H/L tonal with floating tones and says the tone of nominal prefixes could not yet be determined.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. On tone: verbal-radical tone alternance is hidden in the infinitive; vowel length is grammatical, not lexical (§2.5).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone patterns of nouns and verb forms, elicited from one informant (Pierre Lifenya, chefferie Baluolambi, at Yakusu, Dec. 1954); tone patterns are said to hold in all observed syntactic positions.
new_statements.identity_note: Identity needs verification. Harries 1955 describes 'Gesogo (ligesögo)' of the chefferie Baluolambi (chef-lieu Yonange, Yakusu area, south bank of the Congo west of Kisangani to the Lomami) and states on p. 420 'The language is also known as Topoke or Eso'; Stoop 1989 labels his 'sogo' Guthrie C53 and calls it 'le système sogo ou poke' (p. 128) — in Guthrie, C53 is Poke/Topoke while So(ko) of Basoko is C52. Glottolog/hh nevertheless map both Harries 1955 and Stoop 1989 to sode1235 [soc] (EBALL keyword c.52). So the quoted statement may describe Poke/Topoke [pof] = poke1238 rather than So of Basoko; Carrington's 'Baso/Heso' notes (Basoko variety) are the only material here unambiguously from So proper, and they contain no statement. Motingea 2012 (Basoa) is the source that would settle this.

new_statements.translation: §2.2.4 Tones: The language of the Basoa attests simple tones and complex tones. [...] Phonologically, then, there exist only the high tone and the low tone. Phonetically, however, one can perceive three simple tones: high, mid and low. [...] The examples in (34c) show the lexical value of tones in Soa: moto 'man' vs. motó 'head' [...] mwélá 'smoke' vs. mwěla 'tail'. (p. 24) — §6.4 (about the whole Congo-bend region, p. 243): It is, for example, apart from the tonology, a matter of a system of stresses (or rhythm?) consisting in 'dragging out' the realisation of certain prosodic units. This system has unfortunately not yet been the object of any study.

new_statements.relation_note: Language not in the catalog. The existing statement (Harries 1955, Gesogo: lexical tone, no stress statement) is of the same type — tone language, no word-stress statement — so Motingea agrees with it in type. But Motingea himself files Harries 1955 under tofoké C53 (p. 241) and lists 'les Tofoké, connus aussi sous les noms de Sogo et Eso (Harries 1955, Stoop 1989a, Stoop 1989b)' as the southern NEIGHBOURS of the Basoa (p. 15), so the Harries statement most likely belongs to Poke [pof] poke1238, and this Motingea sketch is the first the deciding source that is unambiguously about So/Soa C52. The p. 243 remark is a regional, hedged suggestion of a stress/rhythmic system and does not give a p…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Soa (of Ilondé) is a two-tone language (H vs. L phonologically; a phonetic mid = H realised before L; rising and falling tones arise from vowel contraction or lexicalised consonant loss); tone is lexically contrastive (minimal pairs). The grammar sketch has no section on stress or accent and never states a stress placement; 'accent' occurs only as the name of the acute diacritic. The morphotoneme section describes tonal fusion, tone harmony, tonal polarity, métatonie (final -a of perfect/progressive raised before a following word, lowered phrase-finally, which the author calls 'prosodie phrasale'), Meeussen-type dissimilation, raising, a phonetic downstep of H between two L's ('faille tonale', °BHB > HMB), and a floating L in the prohibitive. The only mention of stress is a hedged regional remark in the closing chapter (p. 243) that the languages of the Congo bend up to the Batetela show, besides tone, a 'system of stresses (or rhythm?)' of lengthening certain prosodic units, never studied.
new_statements.exceptions: None about stress. Tonal notes: the young female informant Angèle Angwadima does not apply the tone-raising rule before connective/possessive (p. 38); the author cannot cleanly separate métatonie from the pausal low tone common to the Aruwimi-Lomamé languages (p. 36).
new_statements.identity_note: Motingea's ch. 2 describes 'la langue des Basoa telle qu'elle est parlée dans la localité d'Ilondé' (Secteur de Yawémbé, Territoire d'Isangi), the Basoa being 'connue aussi sous le nom de Basoko, Basɔkɔ́ selon la phonétique de la langue elle-même' (p. 15), = Guthrie C52 so (= soko) (p. 9); data from Ilongosi Ilonga of Ilondé (Mbandaka, Sept. 1993) checked with Marie Mondondi Mbuli and Angèle Angwandima of the same village (Kinshasa, Oct. 1999). The book's other sketches (Mbesa C51 [zms], Tofoké of Yangole C53 [pof], Lokelé of the Mboosó [khy]) are other languages. Motingea explicitly treats Tofoké = Sogo = Eso (Harries 1955, Stoop 1989a,b) as a neighbouring language, so the existing Harries 1955 statement filed under sode1235 most likely describes Poke [pof].

tone_statements.citation: Carrington, John F. 1971. The musical dimension of perception in the Upper Congo, Zaïre. African Music: Journal of the African Music Society 5(1): 46-51. doi:10.21504/amj.v5i1.1149
tone_statements.quote: Yodelling is frequently heard from fishermen returning to the village after work among the islands of the river. Wishing to send a message to their families while they are still some distance away from the village (a mile or more), they imitate the signals of the gong-language phrases by shouting ke or le for the low-toned syllables and ki or li for the high tones. Fishermen in the Basoko area use a similar yodelled language but in their case we hear ko and o for the low tone and ku and u for the high tone. (p. 48)
tone_statements.locator: p. 48 (Yalemba/Yamoya gong-name with tonic sol-fa high/low notation; Basoko-area fishermen's yodelled tone language: ko/o = low tone, ku/u = high tone), pp. 50-51 (Basoko bird-song phrase 'hae haloa' with its semantic tones); pp. 46-47 two-tone exposition is for Lokele
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Two tones (high/low) presupposed for the Basoko-area language, rendered on two-note gongs and in a two-vowel yodelled surrogate; stated explicitly only for Lokele.

tone_statements.quote: In every case, tonal patterns are identical but phonetic elements change. This phenomenon is observed especially where the linguistic basis of the beaten messages is not the spoken language of the tribe. Gong-phrases learned from a nearby tribe that has "lent" its gong-language to neighbours are learned by the former as tonal units but contain phonetic elements that are not properly understood. It follows that, while the tonal patterns remain constant and have significance for the listener, the phonetic elements vary considerably from one beater to another. (p. 13; p. 10: 'The hollowing under one "cheek" is carried further than that under the other so that the former emits a low-toned note when struck with a rubber-covered stick while the latter gives a higher note. ... Gong-beaters refer to the low-toned note as the "voice of the male"; the other lip gives the "voice of the female".')
tone_statements.locator: pp. 10 (two-note gong: low 'male' / high 'female' lip), 12-13 'Linguistic notes' (tonal patterns constant, phonetic elements variable), 14-17 table of 47 gong-names with high/low beat notation, 40 of them in the (Hɛ)Sɔ gong-language
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Two-level (high vs low) tonal patterns of spoken So carried by a two-note slit-gong; tone patterns are the invariant, meaning-bearing part of each phrase.

tone_statements.quote: B ) The number of tones in Central African languages. The problem of the number of tones in African languages was reviewed by Nekes as an attempted answer to his question : « Gibt es im Bantu verschiedene Tonsvs-teme ? » ( N e k e s , 55, p. 81). The following list of languages inchides some of those given by Nekes as well as others from the area covered by the present investiga-tion : 2 tones reported : Bangi (W hitehead); Luba (Burssens); Ngala (Guthrie); Nkundó and Tumba (Hulstaert); Yaunde (Heepe); Kele Mbole, Ena, Topoke, Olombo, Ar] ba, Komo, So (Carrington).

tone_statements.summary: So reported as a two-tone (H/L) language; gong-language phrases transmit the H/L tonal + rhythmic pattern of spoken So; composite tones = sequences of the two level tones (Carrington's general analysis for the area).
